name: ccache
baseline: Make (uncached GCC recompilation as invoked by Make/Ninja/CMake build loops)
workload: Median of 100 runs compiling ccache's own ccache.c (-g -O2 -MD) and a preprocessor-heavy c++_includes.cc (-MD), comparing no-cache vs ccache's direct/preprocessor/depend cache-hit modes.
claimed_speedup: ccache.c: 145.39x (direct mode), 137.81x (depend mode), 28.33x (preprocessor mode) vs no cache. c++_includes.cc: 29.10x (direct), 29.32x (depend), 5.09x (preprocessor) vs no cache.
hardware: Intel Core i5-4690K, SSD
stars_or_usage: 3.0k stars; bundled/used by default in many Linux distro and CI C/C++ build pipelines
tradeoffs: Only accelerates cache-hit rebuilds; provides no benefit on true cold/clean builds; requires stable compiler/flags/includes for hits; direct mode is disabled by some preprocessor macros (e.g. __TIME__).
caveats: Benchmark measures a single-file cache-hit vs cache-miss GCC compile, not an end-to-end Make/Ninja project build; real-world speedup depends heavily on cache hit rate. CPU (i5-4690K) is a dated part and the page does not state when the benchmark was run.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/ccache/ccache + WebFetch https://ccache.dev/performance.html

name: Mill
workload: Compiling Netty (~500k LOC, 47 submodules) vs Maven, and Mockito (~100k LOC, 22 submodules) vs Gradle: sequential/parallel clean-compile-all, single-module clean/incremental/no-op compile.
claimed_speedup: vs Maven (Netty): 4.0x sequential clean compile all, 4.9x parallel clean compile all, 7.0x clean compile single module, 30.7x incremental single module, 44.0x no-op single module. vs Gradle (Mockito): 3.7x, 3.6x, 5.2x, 5.9x, 10.2x for the same five scenarios.
hardware: M1 MacBook Pro, 10 CPU cores, 32GB RAM
stars_or_usage: 2.8k stars
tradeoffs: JVM-only (Java/Scala/Kotlin), not usable for C++/CMake/Cargo projects; uses Mill's own build.mill DSL instead of pom.xml/build.gradle; smaller plugin ecosystem than Maven or Gradle.
caveats: Baseline is Maven/Gradle, not one of this run's named baselines (CMake+Ninja, Make, Bazel, Cargo); numbers are Mill's own published benchmark, but the exact build configs (example/thirdparty/netty/build.mill and .../mockito/build.mill) are public in the repo for reproduction, satisfying tier-A methodology requirements.

name: tup
workload: Synthetic C project generator (logarithmic directory tree, up to 100,000 C files / ~200,000 total files with headers): cold build, single-file-change rebuild, and no-op ('nothing changed') dependency check, tup vs make.
claimed_speedup: At 100k files: no-op check ~0s (tup) vs ~30 minutes (make); single C-file change rebuild ~0.1s (tup) vs ~30 minutes (make). Cold/initial build: tup is 5-30% SLOWER than make across sizes.
stars_or_usage: 1.3k stars
tradeoffs: Requires all build outputs declared explicitly (no implicit globbing) for correctness; runs a persistent filesystem-watching 'monitor' process; much smaller ecosystem/IDE support than Make/CMake.
caveats: First-party project page with no CPU model, OS, or compiler flags stated, and the ratio (30min vs 0.1s) is implausible-looking, so capped at tier C per the >50x rule. Page footer shows a 2008-2024 copyright range, so hardware is likely old/unstated. The 100k-file case is a stress test, not a typical project size, and tup's own numbers show its cold build is actually slower than make.

name: NativeLink
baseline: local, non-distributed single-machine build (no remote cache / no distributed compilation)
workload: Full LLVM + Clang project build (~4,468 build actions, culminating in llvm-readelf) via CMake+Ninja and the recc REAPI client, comparing a local laptop build to the same build distributed across a home Kubernetes/Talos cluster through NativeLink.
claimed_speedup: Independent blog: full LLVM build dropped from 1026s (~17min, local) to 257.5s (~4.3min, distributed via recc+NativeLink, -j96, PCH disabled) ≈ 4.0x faster; a second local build hitting a warm remote cache completed in 92.9s. NativeLink's own site/docs separately state '4 to 15 times faster builds, demonstrated on LLVM' and 'LLVM builds 4 times faster on NativeLink' (cutting a full build from 17 minutes to 4).
compiler_and_flags: LLVM CI Ubuntu 24.04 container toolchain (LTO/BOLT-optimized clang), CMake + Ninja, -j96, precompiled headers disabled for the primary recc run
hardware: Client: a Framework desktop (exact CPU model not given); server: a home Kubernetes cluster on Talos Linux with several 'OptiBlex' nodes described as low-power, connected via WiFi (later re-tested over VPN)
stars_or_usage: 1.6k stars; vendor claims 10B+ build requests/month in production, used by Samsung and others
tradeoffs: Requires standing up a CAS/remote-execution server (Docker/Kubernetes) rather than a single local binary; core cache is source-available FSL-1.1 (converts to Apache-2.0 two years after each release) and some modules (metrics, persistent-worker) are Business Source License requiring a commercial license for shared production use; integrates via the Bazel Remote Execution API (Bazel, Buck2, reclient/recc, etc.) rather than being a drop-in ccache/distcc substitute.
caveats: Benchmark is by an independent third party (a named ex-Google LLVM/Clang contributor) rather than a peer-reviewed or formal shootout, and does not compare directly against distcc, icecream or ccache — only against a non-distributed local build. Exact CPU models for client and server nodes are not given, which caps this below tier A. The company's own site repeats the number as '4 to 15x' without publishing the wider range's methodology.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/TraceMachina/nativelink (direct lookup of a known Bazel-REAPI-compatible remote cache/execution project); benchmark surfaced via repos/TraceMachina/nativelink/contents/llms-small.txt and its linked post https://reidkleckner.dev/posts/llvm-recc-nativelink/

name: HOMCC
workload: Distributed remote compilation of a Celonis-internal C++ codebase with clang++-14 (total server job limit 112, 60 compilation threads), measuring total remote compilation time across simulated up/download bandwidths from 5/25 Mbps to 1000/1000 Mbps, comparing homcc vs. distcc.
claimed_speedup: README chart 'compilation_times.png' (read visually, approximate): at 5/25 Mbps homcc ~9.2min vs distcc ~57.5min (~6.3x); at 10/50 Mbps ~7.7min vs ~28.8min (~3.7x); at 20/100 Mbps ~6.4min vs ~14.8min (~2.3x); at 40/200 Mbps ~5.8min vs ~7.9min (~1.4x); at 1000/1000 Mbps (gigabit, effectively unconstrained) ~5.8min vs ~4.9min — distcc is slightly faster once bandwidth is no longer the bottleneck (derived from page data / chart, values estimated from bar heights, not printed as text)
compiler_and_flags: clang++-14; server job limit 112, 60 compilation threads
stars_or_usage: 24 stars

caveats: Benchmark uses an internal, non-public Celonis C++ codebase, so it is not independently reproducible; the only numbers are in an embedded chart image with no CPU model stated and no linked raw data or benchmark script, so this stays at tier C. Values above were read off the bar chart, not quoted as exact text, and are explicitly marked as derived/approximate.

name: octobuild
baseline: stock Unreal Build Tool / Unreal Automation Tool build with no distributed cache/accelerator (ccache and distcc do not natively support the MSVC/console toolchains Unreal Engine uses)
workload: Full Unreal Engine 5.0.3 project rebuild (RunUAT.sh/RunUBT.bat, DebugGame config) on Linux, Win64 (MSVC 2019), PS4, PS5, Xbox One and Xbox Series X, comparing no cache vs. octobuild with a cold (0%) and fully warm (100%) cache.
claimed_speedup: README states 60-90% reduction in re-compile time; benchmark table shows, at 100% cache hit vs. no cache: Linux 3m54s→36s (~6.5x), Win64 8m4s→2m15s (~3.6x), PS4 6m12s→2m34s (~2.4x), PS5 5m48s→2m11s (~2.7x), XB1 4m40s→1m39s (~2.8x), XSX 4m49s→1m40s (~2.9x) (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 2019 (Win64), platform-bundled clang toolchains for Linux/PS4/PS5/XB1/XSX; UE5.0.3 DebugGame configuration via RunUAT/RunUBT; exact compiler flags not enumerated
hardware: Linux: AMD Ryzen 7 3700X, 32GB DDR4@3200MHz, SSD. Windows/console: Intel Core i7-9700F, 32GB DDR4@2400MHz, SSD.
stars_or_usage: 285 stars
tradeoffs: UE-specific: requires patches to Unreal Engine on Linux/macOS to enable octobuild; cache is disk-based with a configurable size limit (default 64GB); at 0% cache hit rate it adds measurable overhead over an uncached build (e.g. Win64 went from 8m4s to 10m6s cold) so benefit depends entirely on cache warmth.
caveats: Not benchmarked against ccache, sccache or distcc directly — those tools do not support MSVC/console compilers well, so the only baseline is 'no accelerator'. Numbers come from the project's own README table (first-party), not a published, independently reproducible benchmark harness, and exact compiler flags are not listed, so tier is capped at C despite hardware being named.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "compiler cache" --sort stars --limit 30

name: Intel oneAPI DPC++/C++ Compiler (icpx)
workload: Runtime of a single-threaded equity-volatility quant pipeline (parse ~30M option quotes from a 1 GB pcap, Black-Scholes implied-vol Newton inversion, SVI smile fits, greeks) built with GCC, Clang and icpx from identical source in strict-IEEE and fast-math variants.
claimed_speedup: icpx-fast finishes the pipeline 1.79x faster than gcc-strict (13700 ms vs 24536 ms total) and 1.44x faster than the best non-Intel variant (clang-fast-zmm, 20453 ms). Under strict IEEE the field compresses to 1.00-1.23x (icpx-strict 19920 ms vs gcc-strict 24536 ms vs clang-strict 22475 ms). SVI fit stage 2385 ms vs 8879 ms (3.7x) and greeks 770 ms vs 2571 ms (3.3x) for icpx-fast vs gcc-strict.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 13.3.0 -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops [-ffast-math]; clang 18.1.8 -O3 -march=native [-ffast-math -fveclib=libmvec]; icpx (IntelLLVM 2025.3.3) -O3 -xHost -fp-model=precise (strict) or -fp-model=fast -fimf-precision=high (fast); zmm variants add -mprefer-vector-width=512 or -qopt-zmm-usage=high
hardware: 4-vCPU KVM guest on a 5th-gen Xeon Scalable (Emerald Rapids, family 6 model 207; hypervisor masks the retail SKU), AVX-512 exposed; shared cloud host, single session
license: Apache-2.0 (intel/llvm open-source base); the benchmarked icpx binary came from the proprietary oneapi-basekit image
stars_or_usage: intel/llvm 1.5k stars (open-source base of the oneAPI DPC++ compiler); benchmark repo yzia2000/qr_cpp_compiler 0 stars, 8 commits Aug 1-2 2026
tradeoffs: Most of the gain needs -fp-model=fast (relaxed floating point) and Intel's SVML/libimf vector math; Intel hardware oriented (-xHost); closed-source optimizer components in the shipped product; proprietary terms for the shipped binary.
caveats: Benchmark is a small personal repo (0 stars, no LICENSE file seen, 8 commits in two days) on a transcendental-heavy workload chosen to favour SVML; it is a single session on a shared cloud VM so numbers are relative; CPU SKU is masked (family 6 model 207 stated), so tier A is borderline. The README itself notes gcc-fast beats icpx-fast on the Newton IV stage (3.07 vs 2.83 Mq/s), strict-IEEE advantage is only 1.23x, and forcing 512-bit vectors made icpx 14.8% slower. Corroboration, opened: LAMMPS issue #5213 (author akohlmey, Sept 2026, 2x20-core Xeon Gold 6248 Cascade Lake, RHEL 10, GCC 14 -O3 -march=native -ffast-math vs icpx 2026.1 -xHost -fp-model fast=2, values relative to GCC 14 '-sf intel') reports icpx at lj 1.70, rhodo 1.62, sw 1.85, water 1.88, airebo 1.85, tersoff 1.49, snap 3.48, but lc 0.91 and dpd 1.02, so it is not uniformly faster. Counter-evidence, opened: gist kaityo256/d41481467df504c5039715d38954ab8a (GCC 5.4-9.2 vs ICC 18-19.1 vs Clang 8, -O3 -march=native/-xHOST, four Intel CPUs) shows GCC 40-60x faster on a degenerate std::uniform_real_distribution loop (0.05s vs 2.72s on Xeon Gold 6230). Search-snippet only (pages blocked here, not opened): SPEC withdrew over 2,000 SPEC CPU 2017 results that used a benchmark-specific oneAPI DPC++ optimization, and older ICC-vs-GCC articles show the gap narrowing. The listed 'Intel C++ Compiler' (software.intel.com) is the proprietary product; repo_url points at its open-source base, which is not what was benchmarked.
found_via: seed-record pass; started from https://software.intel.com/en-us/c-compilers (awesome-cpp#Compiler); WebSearch 'icx icpx vs gcc clang benchmark speedup Intel compiler github' surfaced yzia2000/qr_cpp_compiler, lammps issue #5213 and the kaityo256 gist

claimed_speedup: Debug full build (-j1): GCC 5.4.0 469s, Clang 3.9 710s, Zapcc++ 214s -- 'zapcc is 3.3 times faster to compile than Clang and around 2 times faster than GCC'. Release build (-j1): GCC 782s, Clang 960s, Zapcc 640s -- 'zapcc is still 1.2 times faster than gcc and 1.5 times faster than clang'
compiler_and_flags: GCC 5.4.0, Clang 3.9, Zapcc++ (beta); default optimization flags, -j1/-j2/-j4 parallelism, debug and release configurations
hardware: Desktop machine, 4 physical cores, 16GB RAM (exact CPU model not stated)
stars_or_usage: 1.3k stars

name: GCC
workload: Run time of binaries built by GCC 9.2.1 versus Clang 9.0 for 41 C/C++ Phoronix Test Suite benchmarks on an Intel Ice Lake laptop (Ubuntu 19.10).
claimed_speedup: GCC 9.2.1 slightly ahead of Clang 9.0 by geometric mean over 41 benchmarks; Clang reached about 96% of GCC's performance (so GCC about 4% faster, derived from page data). Clang won 22 of the 41 tests (53.6%) and GCC 19.
hardware: Intel Core i7-1065G7 'Ice Lake' (CPU model from a search summary, unverified)
stars_or_usage: 11.3k stars on the gcc-mirror/gcc GitHub mirror; default system compiler of most Linux distributions
tradeoffs: Upstream development is at git://gcc.gnu.org/git/gcc.git, the GitHub repo is a read-only mirror; GPL toolchain (runtime libraries carry the GCC Runtime Library Exception); code-generation lead over Clang is small and workload-dependent.
caveats: Snippet only: gcc.gnu.org, phoronix.com and openbenchmarking.org were EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the numbers come from WebSearch result summaries, not from an opened page; compiler flags unknown. The 2019/2020 data is old, and the lead flips by release and CPU: the 2022 Phoronix Milan-X article had Clang 14.0 about 2% faster than GCC 11.2 by geometric mean, the 2019 62-benchmark study (https://phoronix.com/scan.php?item=gcc-clang-2019&num=1&page=article) had GCC about 2% faster on an FX-8370E and only a few percent on newer Intel CPUs, and the 2025 'GCC 15 vs LLVM Clang 20' Zen 5 article (https://www.phoronix.com/review/clang20-gcc15-amd-znver5) reports GCC 14/15 with a 'very small' geometric-mean win over Clang 19/20 (no exact figure seen). The honest summary is rough parity with a few percent either way, not a clear speed win. GCC is itself the incumbent baseline for most other entries in compilers-frontends.

name: MIR / c2m (C2MIR)
workload: Compiling a single C function (Eratosthenes sieve, no #include headers) via the c2m JIT front-end vs gcc -O2/-O0, with gcc run against an in-memory filesystem to remove disk I/O
claimed_speedup: c2m -eg compiles in 336us vs gcc -O2 in 27.1ms (~80x) and gcc -O0 in 26.1ms (~77x); c2m-generated code then runs at about 92% of gcc -O2 speed on the same benchmark
hardware: Intel i5-13600K, 64GB RAM, Fedora 37
stars_or_usage: 2.6k stars
tradeoffs: c2m targets lightweight JIT use cases: a short optimization pipeline, partial C11 + GCC-extension coverage, and no full preprocessor handling of complex real-world header trees in the quoted benchmark; general-purpose builds would see a smaller gap than the single-function test implies
caveats: This is the project's own README benchmark table (first-party with stated methodology), which per the rules is Tier C, not B. The workload is a single tiny function with zero #include files, and gcc is forced through a memory filesystem to remove I/O -- a best case for a minimal front-end, not representative of typical multi-file/header-heavy C builds. The table also directly compares against gcc -O0, which independently caps the tier at C; an 80x ratio is plausible only for this narrow synthetic case.

name: mold
workload: Linking 9 large real-world programs (Blender, Chromium, Clang, ClickHouse, Firefox, Godot, LibreOffice, PyTorch, TensorFlow, some also in ARM64 variants) in both debug and release configurations, on an AMD Ryzen Threadripper 7980X (Ubuntu 24.04) and an Apple M1 Ultra (Fedora Asahi Remix 42); wall-clock time, median of 3 runs after a warm-up run.
claimed_speedup: 4.9x faster than LLVM lld and 1.9x faster than wild at the median (August 2026 benchmark); per-program lld/mold ratios in the published table range from ~1.5x up to 16.1x depending on program/build-type/machine (e.g. TensorFlow debug on Threadripper: 50.73s (lld) -> 3.15s (mold) = 16.1x; Blender release on M1 Ultra: 0.56s (lld) -> 0.25s (mold) = 2.3x)
compiler_and_flags: All three linkers (lld, wild, mold) built from source 'in release configuration' as of 2026-08-28 and run with default options; exact compiler/version and flags used to compile the 9 benchmarked programs themselves are not enumerated in the README, only that debug vs. release build variants were both tested.
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 7980X (64 cores), Ubuntu 24.04; Apple M1 Ultra (16 performance + 4 efficiency cores, benchmark restricted to performance cores), Fedora Asahi Remix 42
stars_or_usage: 17.2k stars; default linker for many large open-source projects, in production use since 2021 (author is the original developer of LLVM lld)
tradeoffs: As of the current main branch mold has been rewritten from C++ to Rust (confirmed via repo language metadata, README build instructions requiring Cargo, and the author's own Sept 2026 announcement); no incremental linking; supports x86-64/i386/ARM32/64/RISC-V32/64/PowerPC32/64/s390x/LoongArch32/64/SPARC64/m68k/SH-4 but has no native Windows/MSVC target; on the M1 Ultra debug-build table, mold is actually slower than lld for Clang (0.9x, i.e. a regression on that one workload).
caveats: Numbers are published in mold's own README (self-reported by the mold maintainer), though the benchmark suite/inputs are archived publicly on Zenodo (https://zenodo.org/records/21882261) and hardware, OS, date, and run methodology (median of 3, warm-up) are stated, meeting tier-A code+hardware requirements; exact compiler/flags for the 9 test programs are not itemized. The comparison table only includes lld and wild, not GNU ld (bfd) or gold directly, even though the README's intro claims mold is a 'drop-in replacement for existing Unix linkers' generally.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "mold linker" --sort stars; gh api repos/rui314/mold and repos/rui314/mold/readme; corroborated via HN Algolia search "wild linker mold" (Phoronix: "Wild: A Fast Linker Written in Rust, Aims to Outperform Mold Linker")

workload: Same 9-program benchmark suite as mold's README (Blender, Chromium, Clang, ClickHouse, Firefox, Godot, LibreOffice, PyTorch, TensorFlow) linked in debug and release configurations on an AMD Ryzen Threadripper 7980X and an Apple M1 Ultra; wild lacks --icf=all (identical code folding) support, so several rows (e.g. Chromium release, TensorFlow, Firefox) are marked N/A for wild in that table.
claimed_speedup: In mold's third-party comparison table, wild links faster than lld on most rows where it is supported, e.g. (debug, Threadripper) Blender 4.72s(lld)->1.98s(wild)=2.4x, ClickHouse 6.62s->4.40s=1.5x, Godot 1.77s->1.08s=1.6x (all derived from page data); wild's own BENCHMARKING.md documents a local hyperfine run on ripgrep showing wild ~10.9x faster than GNU ld and ~1.7x faster than mold, but that specific figure is explicitly presented as an illustrative example ('with different values'), not a reported result.

Newer linkers such as mold are faster than lld. llvm-project is already in the catalog (AddressSanitizer entry), so this lld record needs a distinct id or paper: key before merge. name: RapidProto
workload: Decoding a realistic 2000-record mixed Dataset payload (strings, nested/repeated messages, packed scalar arrays) serialized by protoc, plus protobuf's own google_message1/google_message2 corpora and a 20MB OpenStreetMap PBF extract
claimed_speedup: ~7x faster arena decode than protoc+google::protobuf::Arena (g++-13; ~6x on clang++-20), with ~0.49x peak payload memory; streaming decoder ~12x faster than protoc+Arena and ~1.8x faster than protozero; +61% MB/s vs protoc on the OSM PBF protobuf-layer decode
stars_or_usage: 3 stars (new project, created 2026-06-28)
tradeoffs: Decode-only (no serialization/mutation); arena tree strings/bytes/raw payloads are borrowed views into the input, so they stay valid only while both the input and the Arena outlive them; does not validate string UTF-8 (protoc does); enums decode as open even when the schema declares them closed
caveats: CPU model is not stated in the benchmarks doc (only 'quiesced box' with core pinning) even though compiler, flags, and protobuf version are, so this is capped at tier B rather than A. Very new, low-star project; numbers come from the project's own reproducible harness, not an independent third party.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "faster than protoc"

name: FlatBuffers
workload: Decode+Traverse+Dealloc and Encode of a ~10-object benchmark structure (an array, 4 strings, assorted int/float scalars), 1 million iterations, C++ on Windows 7 64-bit, FlatBuffers binary format vs the Protocol Buffers LITE C++ runtime generated by protoc
claimed_speedup: Decode+Traverse+Dealloc: 0.08s (FlatBuffers) vs 302s (Protobuf LITE) per 1M iterations, ~3775x (derived from page data); Encode: 3.2s vs 185s, ~58x (derived from page data)
hardware: Windows 7 64-bit (no CPU model stated)
stars_or_usage: 26.5k stars; used across Google, Unity, Facebook and many game engines
tradeoffs: FlatBuffers reads fields in-place without unpacking, trading a full mutable object model for speed; its wire format is larger than Protobuf's for this benchmark object (344B vs 228B); lacks Protobuf's per-field forward/backward compatibility bookkeeping cost, which is part of why decode is cheaper
caveats: Benchmark text says only 'running on Windows 7 64bit' (no compiler, flags, or CPU model given), is clearly old (Windows 7 era), and the >3000x decode ratio is implausible for two optimized libraries, most likely reflecting a debug/unoptimized protobuf build. Capped at tier C under the >50x-implausible rule; no more recent published benchmark was found in the repo within this session's budget.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/google/flatbuffers/contents/docs/source/benchmarks.md, checked directly as a known protoc-competing code generator not on the excluded list

name: vtprotobuf (protoc-gen-go-vtproto)
workload: Marshal/Unmarshal/Size/Equal/Clone of arbitrary Protobuf messages: vtprotobuf runs as an auxiliary protoc plugin alongside protoc-gen-go, generating fully unrolled, reflection-free Go (de)serialization code
claimed_speedup: Qualitative only: README states the generated methods behave like the standard proto.Marshal/Unmarshal/Size/Equal/Clone calls 'except...fully unrolled and does not use reflection' and with fewer/no allocations; no numeric multiplier found in the repo's own docs during this session
stars_or_usage: 1118 stars; used in production by Vitess/PlanetScale and adopted widely in the Go gRPC ecosystem
tradeoffs: Generates auxiliary *_vtproto.pb.go helpers that must be explicitly opted into (SizeVT/MarshalVT/UnmarshalVT etc.) rather than replacing standard methods; the 'unsafe' unmarshal variant aliases input bytes into strings, requiring the caller to keep the wire buffer alive; adds a build-time dependency on the vtproto plugin
caveats: No benchmark numbers were found in the README, and a targeted search for a blog post or independent write-up with numbers (HN, Planetscale blog) turned up nothing this session, despite the project's explicit framing as a reflection-avoiding, allocation-reducing alternative to protoc-gen-go. Recorded as tier D under the notability exception (>1k stars, widely referenced). A dedicated numeric benchmark may exist but was not located within budget.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "faster than protoc" led to checking Go protoc-gen-go alternatives, then gh api repos/planetscale/vtprotobuf
